scenes.heading: Carbonyl compounds
scenes.sub: One group, two patterns: add or substitute
scenes.say: The C O double bond is in sugars, proteins, fats and aspirin. Once you see why its carbon is electron-poor, a huge family of reactions collapses into just two patterns: addition and substitution.
scenes.caption: The C=O group is in sugars, proteins, fats and aspirin. Once you see why its carbon is electron-poor, a huge family of reactions collapses into just two patterns: addition and substitution.

scenes.heading: The carbonyl group
points: C is sp², trigonal planar, about 120°
O is δ−, C is δ+: an electrophile
scenes.say: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbonyl carbon is delta positive. That makes it an electrophile for nucleophiles to attack. It's flat, so attack can come from either face.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Someone squeezes into a full lift; does anyone step out?
scenes.science: Nucleophile adds: tetrahedral intermediate. Leaving group? Substitution
scenes.breaks: the nucleophile is drawn to the δ+ carbon, not to spare room, and the leaving group leaves in a separate later step.
scenes.say: Picture a full lift. A nucleophile squeezes in, making a crowded tetrahedral intermediate. If someone near the door can step out, a leaving group like chloride, they leave and the C O double bond re-forms. That's substitution. If nobody can leave, as in aldehydes and ketones, the newcomer stays. That's addition.
scenes.caption: Picture a full lift. A nucleophile squeezes in, making a crowded tetrahedral intermediate. If someone can step out, a leaving group like Cl⁻, they leave and the C=O re-forms. That's substitution. If nobody can leave, as in aldehydes and ketones, the newcomer stays. That's addition.

scenes.heading: Addition vs acyl substitution

left.title: Nucleophilic addition
points: Only H or C attached: can't leave

right.title: Acyl substitution
points: Cl, OR or NR₂ can leave

scenes.say: Can it leave? Then substitute. If not, add. In addition, the C O disappears and you get an alcohol. In acyl substitution, the nucleophile adds, then the leaving group departs, and the C O is kept.
scenes.caption: Can it leave? Then substitute. If not, add. In addition, the C=O disappears and you get an alcohol. In acyl substitution, the nucleophile adds, then the leaving group departs, and the C=O is kept.

scenes.heading: Reactivity: Clever Animals Eat Apples
scenes.say: Clever animals eat apples: acid chloride, anhydride, ester, amide, from most to least reactive. Chloride is a weak base, so it's a great leaving group. Nitrogen shares its lone pair with the C O, so amides are very stable. You can slide down this list, but not climb back up.
scenes.caption: Clever Animals Eat Apples: acid chloride, anhydride, ester, amide, from most to least reactive. Cl⁻ is a weak base, so it's a great leaving group. N shares its lone pair with the C=O, so amides are very stable. You can slide down this list, but not climb back up.

scenes.heading: Worked example: a Grignard
scenes.question: Propanone reacts with ethylmagnesium bromide, then aqueous acid. Name the product.
lines: Ethyl group adds to the δ+ carbonyl carbon
scenes.say: The Grignard delivers an ethyl group to the carbonyl carbon, making an alkoxide. Acid work-up turns it into an alcohol: two methyl butan two ol. A ketone plus a Grignard always gives a tertiary alcohol.
scenes.caption: The Grignard delivers an ethyl group to the carbonyl carbon, making an alkoxide. Acid work-up turns it into an alcohol: 2-methylbutan-2-ol. A ketone plus a Grignard always gives a tertiary alcohol.

points: Carbonyl carbon is δ+: an electrophile
Can it leave? Substitute. If not, add
scenes.say: Quick recap. The carbonyl carbon is an electrophile. Can it leave? Then substitute; if not, add. Reactivity runs chloride, anhydride, ester, amide. And always ask: did the C O stay or disappear? Now try the practice questions!
